prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting shape productivity, the pattern of trade and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: B020 remains my preferred single-part prize after the exchange. The case is a model built to be taken to data. Melitz (2003) moved trade analysis from the industry to the firm, and it generated sharp predictions about selection, exit and reallocation that firm-level datasets could confront directly. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) added the exporting-versus-FDI margin. Over two decades the framework has become the standard base for empirical trade, and it has spread to industrial organisation and quantitative macro and into the evaluation of trade agreements. Maturity is not a concern, and the Melitz-Helpman pairing identifies the core model and its first major extension without stretching credit across a large team. The round-1 exchange sharpened the question for me. Several members, including B001 supporters, concede that B020 has the wider footprint in data and estimation. B020 supporters concede that B001 has the cleaner attribution. The disagreement is therefore about weighting, not about the facts. I weight a contribution that changed what is measured and how policy is evaluated above one whose influence runs mainly through the framework. I hold that as a judgement with moderate confidence. I do not count the 2008 gap in trade, or the number of colleagues ranking a candidate first, as merit.
statement.case_against: The attribution boundary is the main weakness. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum supplied firm-level empirical facts and closely related models, and they are not on the credited list, so a Melitz-Helpman award could be read as under-crediting the empirical origins. I cannot repair that by adding uncredited names. Some welfare conclusions depend on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand, which weakens the quantitative side of the case more than the qualitative mechanism. Helpman is also credited on B001, so any trade award forces a choice about which body of his work is recognised. B001 has cleaner attribution and equal maturity. Hjalmarsson's argument that mixed test results are normal for a testable framework has narrowed my discount for B001's empirical record, and the remaining gap between the two candidates is less than I implied in round 1.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first. She argues that mixed results in applications are the normal outcome for a framework with testable predictions, and that the committee should separate contested magnitudes from no lasting contribution. She also says B020 has a less settled attribution than B001.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and it moves me. Protection for sale gave empiricists a structural equation to estimate, and uneven estimates do not show the framework failed. I therefore no longer treat the empirical record as a strong mark against B001, and I rank it as my first alternative. I still weigh B020 higher, because its central mechanisms of selection and reallocation have been confirmed repeatedly in micro data and have changed measurement practice. Your attribution point is fair. I treat it as a real risk for B020, not as a reason to stop at B001. The difference between us is how to weigh attribution cleanliness against measured empirical consequences.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first and wants it to stand on protection for sale and the trade-innovation-growth models, not on Helpman's B020 credit. He ranks B020 below B001 mainly because the omitted empirical pioneers would invite a priority dispute.
responses.response: I agree that each case must stand alone and that Helpman should not act as a bridge between them. That is the standard I apply to B020. On priority, the dispute risk is real, but I read the omitted names as a drafting problem and not as a disqualifier. The conceptual step of selection into exporting is most clearly Melitz's, and Helpman's extension to FDI is the natural second name. The Scientific Background and a mechanism-centred citation can describe the empirical precursors without claiming the firm-level literature is exhausted. My answer to the chair's question is that I would accept B001 as a single-part award, and it is my clear second choice among trade options.

responses.point: Hassler asked that the case for B020 be stated against B001 directly, and not by treating Helpman as a bridge. His own file ranks B016 first and now takes the empirical reorientation toward firm-level data seriously.
responses.response: Stated directly, B020 beats B001 for me on three points: empirical traction, spillover into industrial organisation and quantitative macro, and the reach into policy evaluation. B001 beats B020 on attribution and on the conceptual generality of its mechanism. I weigh the first three more heavily, and I can see how a member could weigh them the other way. I have not checked this against B016, since I did not rank it, and I am not claiming B020 is stronger on merit than a programme I have not assessed as carefully. I take your point that B016's identification is weaker than that of design-based work. That does not change my ordering.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B016 first with moderate confidence and calls B001 the closest rival. He argues the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a substantial gap under a three-name cap, and that B001 is the cleaner trade award.
responses.response: I agree the gap is substantial, and I list it as the main risk to my configuration. I do not think a three-name cap makes the Melitz-Helpman award a prize that leaves out co-originators of the model. The model and its first major extension belong to the two named people, and the empirical precursors are a separate contribution that the citation should not claim. I also note your point that B031 is safer as a Kiyotaki-Moore pair than with Gertler added, and I agree. That is why my B031 alternative remains a two-name version.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B020 first with moderate confidence on the credit gap. He is unsure whether the omission is disqualifying and says it cannot be repaired by adding uncredited names. He also notes that Redding's quantitative and spatial work extends the core.
responses.response: We reach the same configuration with different degrees of doubt, so I should say where I stand. I lean towards the omission not being disqualifying, with moderate confidence. I also change one position from round 1: I would no longer describe a three-name version with Redding as defensible alongside the narrower award. His contribution is later and builds on an established framework, and adding him would blur the conceptual step. I keep the pair at two names. If the Committee wants an award that reaches quantitative practice, that is a different judgement from this one.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is disqualifying for a Melitz-Helpman award. I lean towards no, but with only moderate confidence.
How robust the gains-from-trade conclusions are to parametric assumptions about the productivity distribution and demand, and how much that should count against the empirical side of the case.

Whether the Committee prefers to recognise Helpman for the firm-heterogeneity strand or for the political-economy and growth strand. I see them as separate decisions and do not propose crediting him in two parts.

How to weigh design-based credibility, framework breadth and cumulative field-building under one common criterion. My weighting favours measured empirical consequences, and other members could apply the same criterion differently.
For B031, whether the 2022 prize leaves enough marginal case for Kiyotaki and Moore, and where the collateral-amplification origin ends and the financial-accelerator line begins.
I have not independently verified priority claims or citations. My assessments rest on recollection and on the colleagues' written round-1 positions.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Melitz, Helpman, Grossman or the other credited names on B020 or B001 appears in my supplied profile. My field is corporate finance, venture capital, private equity and financial contracting, which is not close to trade. My alternative B031 involves John Moore, whose work on collateral constraints sits near financial contracting and incomplete-contracts theory, the area I work in. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to him or to the other credited names on B031, and I disclose the thematic adjacency without adjudicating it. I have long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson, and I am Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. These are ties to colleagues and to the Academy, not to any candidate. I have no other update to my round-1 disclosure.
